name: Intention Superiority Effect
summary: Intended but not yet performed actions remain more accessible in memory than completed actions or actions you never intended to do.
explanation:
The Intention Superiority Effect is the finding that information related to actions you intend to perform stays more active in memory than information about actions you have already done or never planned to do. It was demonstrated by Thomas Goschke and Julius Kuhl in 1993.

## The Original Research

Participants learned scripts of everyday activities (such as setting a table), then were told that they would later have to perform one of them and only watch another. In recognition tests, words from the to-be-performed script were recognized faster than words from the other script. The intention made the related information more accessible.

## Why It Matters

The effect is a modern, memory-based confirmation of what Kurt Lewin called a quasi-need: an unfulfilled intention keeps a mental representation active. It is closely related to the Zeigarnik Effect (better memory for unfinished tasks) and the Ovsiankina Effect (the drive to resume them). It also helps explain how prospective memory works: intentions stay 'warm' so that relevant cues can trigger them.

Once the intention is fulfilled, the heightened accessibility disappears, and can even turn into inhibition. That is why you sometimes forget details of a task right after finishing it.

## Practical Implications

- **Open intentions cost something**: Each pending intention keeps information active, which uses attention. Many open intentions add up to mental clutter.
- **Capture to release**: Writing intentions down in a trusted system, with a specific plan, reduces how much they need to stay active in your head.
- **Use it deliberately**: Forming a clear intention before a meeting or a reading session primes you to notice relevant information.
- **Finish to forget**: Completing or explicitly cancelling a task lets your mind release it.

references.title: Goschke, T., & Kuhl, J. (1993). Representation of intentions: Persisting activation in memory. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 19(5), 1211-1226
